An approach in which the solution form of $\gamma$ is guessed follows below. There is some rationality behind the representation of $\gamma$. However, knowing the answer certainly helps. The first step is to make the substitution

$$
\begin{equation*}
x=-(c / 2) \cos \mathcal{X}, \xi=-(c / 2) \cos \theta \tag{6.77}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\chi$ and $\theta$ vary between 0 and $\pi$. The assumed representation of $\gamma$ is

$$
\begin{equation*}
\gamma(\xi)=2 U\left\{a_{0} \frac{1+\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n} \sin n \theta\right\} . \tag{6.78}
\end{equation*}
$$

This vortex density is consistent with the Kutta condition, that is, $\gamma$ is zero at $\theta=\pi$ or $\xi=c / 2$. If $a_{0} \neq 0$, then $\gamma$ is infinite at the leading edge, that is, at $\theta=0$ or $\xi=-c / 2$. It will turn out that the singular term in eq. (6.78) represents the complete solution for a flat plate with an angle of attack. Eq. (6.74) can now be expressed as

$$
\begin{align*}
& \frac{1}{\pi} P V \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\left\{a_{0}(1+\cos \theta)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n} \sin n \theta \cdot \sin \theta\right\}}{\cos \theta-\cos \chi} d \theta \\
& =\eta^{\prime}(x) \tag{6.79}
\end{align*}
$$

The trigonometric identity

$$
\begin{equation*}
\sin n \theta \cdot \sin \theta=\frac{1}{2}[\cos (n-1) \theta-\cos (n+1) \theta] \tag{6.80}
\end{equation*}
$$

is then introduced in eq. (6.79). This will in eq. (6.79) require the evaluation of the Glauert integrals (Newman 1977), that is, that

$$
\begin{equation*}
P V \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\cos n \theta d \theta}{\cos \theta-\cos \chi}=\pi \frac{\sin n \chi}{\sin \chi} . \tag{6.81}
\end{equation*}
$$

It means by using trigonometric identities that

$$
\begin{align*}
P V & \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin n \theta \sin \theta}{\cos \theta-\cos \chi} d \theta \\
= & \frac{1}{2}\left[P V \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\cos (n-1) \theta}{\cos \theta-\cos \chi} d \theta\right. \\
& \left.-P V \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\cos (n+1) \theta}{\cos \theta-\cos \chi} d \theta\right] \\
= & \frac{\pi}{2}\left[\frac{\sin (n-1) \chi-\sin (n+1) \chi}{\sin \chi}\right] \\
= & -\pi \cos n \chi \tag{6.82}
\end{align*}
$$

Eq. (6.79) then becomes

$$
\begin{equation*}
a_{0}-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n} \cos n \chi=\eta^{\prime}(x) \tag{6.83}
\end{equation*}
$$

This is just a Fourier cosine series representation of $\eta^{\prime}(x)$. Because we can always represent $\eta^{\prime}(x)$ like that, the assumed solution form of $\gamma$ is consistent with both the Kutta condition and a Fourier series representation of $\eta^{\prime}(x)$. It follows by multiplying eq. (6.83) with $\cos n \chi, n=0, \ldots$, and integrating from 0 to $\pi$ that

$$
\begin{align*}
& a_{0}=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} \eta^{\prime}(x) d \chi \\
& a_{n}=-\frac{2}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} \eta^{\prime}(x) \cos n \chi d \chi \tag{6.84}
\end{align*}
$$

where $x$ is $-0.5 c \cos \chi$.
When $\gamma(x)$ is obtained, we can find the linearized pressure $p$ on the foil. This follows from eq. (6.59) by noting that $-0.5 \rho\left(u^{2}+v^{2}\right)$ is nonlinear. Because the ambient pressure $p_{a}$ does not contribute to integrated loads on the foil, we disregard $p_{a}$. This gives $p=-\rho U u$ or that

$$
\begin{equation*}
p^{ \pm}= \pm \rho U \frac{\gamma(x)}{2} \tag{6.85}
\end{equation*}
$$

The lift force on the foil is then

$$
\begin{equation*}
L=-\rho U \int_{-c / 2}^{c / 2} \gamma(\xi) d \xi \equiv-\rho U \Gamma \tag{6.86}
\end{equation*}
$$

This is consistent with eq. (6.62). Using eqs. (6.77), (6.78), and (6.84) gives

$$
\begin{align*}
L & =-\rho U \int_{0}^{\pi} \gamma 0.5 c \sin \theta d \theta  \tag{6.87}\\
& =-2 \rho U^{2} \pi\left(a_{0}+0.5 a_{1}\right) 0.5 c
\end{align*}
$$

that is,

$$
L=-2 \rho U^{2}\left(\frac{c}{2}\right) \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{d \eta}{d \xi}(1-\cos \theta) d \theta
$$

We now use eq. (6.77) once more and that $d \xi= c / 2 \sin \theta d \theta=\sqrt{(c / 2)^{2}-\xi^{2}} d \theta$. This implies

$$
\begin{equation*}
L=-2 \rho U^{2} \int_{-c / 2}^{c / 2} \frac{d \eta}{d \xi}\left[\frac{c / 2+\xi}{c / 2-\xi}\right]^{1 / 2} d \xi \tag{6.88}
\end{equation*}
$$

The hydrodynamic moment on the foil about $x=0$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{equation*}
M=-\rho U \int_{-c / 2}^{c / 2} \gamma(\xi) \xi d \xi \tag{6.89}
\end{equation*}
$$

by means of eq. (6.85). This can be rewritten in a similar way as for the lift, that is,

$$
\begin{align*}
M & =\rho U(c / 2)^{2} \int_{0}^{\pi} \gamma \cos \theta \sin \theta d \theta \\
& =\rho 2 U^{2}\left(\frac{c}{2}\right)^{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}\left(a_{0}+\frac{1}{2} a_{2}\right) \tag{6.90}
\end{align*}
$$

Introducing eq. (6.84) now gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
M=2 \rho U^{2} \int_{-c / 2}^{c / 2} \frac{d \eta}{d \xi}\left[(c / 2)^{2}-\xi^{2}\right]^{1 / 2} d \xi \tag{6.91}
\end{equation*}
$$

The center of pressure, $x_{c p}$ is the ratio $x_{c p}= M / L$, that is, the ratio between the hydrodynamic moment $M$ about $x=0$ and the lift force $L$.

### 6.6.1 Flat plate

A flat plate with angle of attack $\alpha$ is considered, that is, $d \eta / d \xi=-\alpha$ in eqs. (6.88) and (6.91). The integrals are evaluated by introducing a new variable $\theta$ so that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\xi=0.5 c \sin \theta \tag{6.92}
\end{equation*}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{gathered}
L=2 \rho U^{2} \alpha \int_{-\pi / 2}^{\pi / 2} \frac{c / 2+(c / 2) \sin \theta}{\left[(c / 2)^{2}-(c / 2)^{2} \sin ^{2} \theta\right]^{1 / 2}} \\
\times(c / 2) \cos \theta d \theta
\end{gathered}
$$

or

$$
\begin{equation*}
L=\rho U^{2} c \pi \alpha \tag{6.93}
\end{equation*}
$$

We could, of course, also use the transformation given by eq. (6.92) to facilitate the integration. The lift coefficient is

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{L}=\frac{L}{0.5 \rho U^{2} c}=2 \pi \alpha \tag{6.94}
\end{equation*}
$$

The moment $M$ can be expressed as

$$
M=-2 \rho U^{2} \alpha(0.5 c)^{2} \int_{-0.5 \pi}^{0.5 \pi} \cos ^{2} \theta d \theta
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-214.jpg?height=611&width=679&top_left_y=191&top_left_x=839)
Figure 6.38. Linear pressure distribution on the top (suction) and bottom (pressure) sides of a flat plate with a positive angle of attack $\alpha . c=$ chord length. Ambient pressure is not included.

or

$$
\begin{equation*}
M=-0.25 \rho U^{2} c^{2} \pi \alpha \tag{6.95}
\end{equation*}
$$

The moment coefficient is then

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{M}=\frac{M}{0.5 \rho U^{2} c^{2}}=-\frac{\pi}{2} \alpha \tag{6.96}
\end{equation*}
$$

This gives that the center of pressure is $0.75 c$ from the trailing edge.

The vortex distribution can be found by eqs. (6.78) and (6.84). It follows from eq. (6.84) that $a_{0}=-\alpha$ and $a_{n}=0$ for $n \geq 1$. Eq. (6.78) with $x$ as a variable instead of $\xi$ gives then that

$$
\gamma=-2 U \alpha \frac{1+\cos \chi}{\sin \chi}=-2 U \alpha \frac{0.5 c-x}{\sqrt{(0.5 c)^{2}-x^{2}}},
$$

that is,

$$
\begin{equation*}
\gamma(x)=-2 \alpha U\left[\frac{0.5 c-x}{0.5 c+x}\right]^{1 / 2} \tag{6.97}
\end{equation*}
$$

We can then use eq. (6.85) to express the pressure on the top and bottom of the foil, that is,

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{p^{ \pm}}{0.5 \rho U^{2} \alpha}=\mp 2\left[\frac{0.5 c-x}{0.5 c+x}\right]^{1 / 2} \tag{6.98}
\end{equation*}
$$

This is illustrated in Figure 6.38. The pressure is infinite at the leading edge. However, the linearized solution is a good approximation of the pressure distribution away from the close vicinity of the leading edge. The flow can be corrected and made finite at the leading edge (Lighthill 1951).

The pressure given by eq. (6.98) is integrably singular at $x=-c / 2$, so the forces and moments are finite as we have already seen by eqs. (6.93) and (6.95).

### 6.6.2 Foil with angle of attack and camber

The camber $\eta_{f}(x)$ of a foil section is measured relative to the nose-tail line (see Figure 6.3). The maximum $f$ of $\eta_{f}(x)$ is called the physical camber. If we represent the camber by a parabola and the foil has an angle of attack $\alpha$ relative to the nose-tail line, we can express the mean line of the foil as

$$
\begin{equation*}
\eta=-\alpha x+f \cdot\left(1-\left(\frac{x}{0.5 c}\right)^{2}\right) \tag{6.99}
\end{equation*}
$$

Because the problem is linear, the effect of the angle of attack $\alpha$ and of the camber can be handled separately. We therefore set $\alpha$ equal to zero first. Using eq. (6.88) gives the lift force as

$$
L=\frac{16 \rho U^{2} f}{c^{2}} \int_{-0.5 c}^{0.5 c} \xi\left[\frac{0.5 c+\xi}{0.5 c-\xi}\right]^{1 / 2} d \xi
$$

Introducing the $\theta$-variable by eq. (6.92), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
L & =4 \rho U^{2} f \int_{-0.5 \pi}^{0.5 \pi} \sin \theta(1+\sin \theta) d \theta \\
& =2 \rho U^{2} f \pi
\end{aligned}
$$

The lift coefficient is then

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{L}=\frac{L}{0.5 \rho U^{2} c}=4 \pi \frac{f}{c} \tag{6.100}
\end{equation*}
$$

This means, for instance, that a small camber ratio $f / c=0.2 / 4 \pi=0.0159$ gives a lift coefficient as large as 0.2 when the angle of attack is zero. Accounting for both the angle of attack $\alpha$ and camber gives then

$$
\begin{equation*}
L=\rho U^{2} c \pi(\alpha+2 f / c) \tag{6.101}
\end{equation*}
$$

where eq. (6.93) has been used for the angle of attack effect. This means zero lift occurs when $\alpha=\alpha_{0}=-2 f / c$. A parabolic camber will not contribute to the moment. Further, the pressure due to the parabolic camber will be finite everywhere along the foil.

### 6.6.3 Ideal angle of attack and angle of attack with zero lift

An angle of attack is called ideal if the linear theory predicts finite pressure at the leading edge. This is also called shockless entry. The constant $a_{0}$ in eq. (6.84) is zero at the ideal angle of attack $\alpha_{i}$. This leads to a vortex distribution (see eq. (6.78)) and a pressure distribution (see eq. (6.85)) that are finite everywhere. Because large negative pressure implies the possibility of cavitation, the ideal angle of attack is important in minimizing the risk for cavitation inception. If we express the mean line of the foil as $\eta=-\alpha x+\eta_{f}(x)$, then eq. (6.84) gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
\alpha_{i}=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} \eta_{f}^{\prime}(x) d \chi \tag{6.102}
\end{equation*}
$$

for a foil in infinite fluid. Here $x=-0.5 c \cos \chi$. The ideal angle of attack is therefore zero for a foil with a camber that is even in $x$. The previous case with a parabolic camber is an example of that.

The angle of attack $\alpha_{0}$ that causes zero lift follows from eqs. (6.87) and (6.84), that is,

$$
\begin{equation*}
\alpha_{0}=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} \eta_{f}^{\prime}(x)(1-\cos \chi) d \chi \tag{6.103}
\end{equation*}
$$

The linear lift coefficient can then be expressed as

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{L}=2 \pi\left(\alpha-\alpha_{0}\right) . \tag{6.104}
\end{equation*}
$$

We saw in Section 6.6.2 that $\alpha_{0}=-2 f / c$ for a foil with parabolic camber.

Let us consider as another example the mean line of the NACA 08 (modified) section (Abbott and von Doenhoff 1959). This is commonly used in the design of conventional propellers. The number 08 means that the vortex density $\gamma$ is constant from the leading edge downstream over a distance 0.8 times the chord length. Using eqs. (6.102) and (6.103) gives $\alpha_{i}=1.40^{\circ}$ and $\alpha_{0}=-7.72^{\circ}$. The lift coefficient at the ideal angle of attack is $2 \pi(1.4+7.72)(\pi / 180)=1$.

### 6.6.4 Weissinger's "quarter-three-quarter-chord" approximation

According to Weissinger's (1942) theory, the circulation $\Gamma$ around a 2D foil in steady motion in infinite fluid can be determined by placing a vortex with strength $\Gamma$ at one quarter of a chord length from the leading edge and satisfying the boundary

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-216.jpg?height=122&width=679&top_left_y=191&top_left_x=136)
Figure 6.39. Foil with a flap of length $r c$ and angle $\alpha_{f}$.

condition at three quarters of a chord length from the leading edge. If this is applied to a foil with angle of attack and camber as described by eq. (6.99), it means that

$$
\frac{\Gamma}{2 \pi 0.5 c}=-U(\alpha+2 f / c) .
$$

Using the Kutta-Joukowski formula for the lift, that is, eq. (6.62), gives the same result as eq. (6.101).

### 6.6.5 Foil with flap

The foil with flap illustrated in Figure 6.39 is considered. The camber is zero. The flap has an angle of attack $\alpha_{f}$ and a length $r c$, where $c$ is the chord length including the flap. The other part of the foil has a zero angle of attack. Using eq. (6.88) to calculate the lift gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
L=2 \rho U^{2} \alpha_{f} \int_{0.5 c-r c}^{0.5 c}\left[\frac{0.5 c+\xi}{0.5 c-\xi}\right]^{1 / 2} d \xi \tag{6.105}
\end{equation*}
$$

We introduce $\theta$ as an integration variable by means of eq. (6.92). When $\xi=0.5 c-r c$, the corresponding angle $\theta$ is $0.5 \pi-\theta_{f}$, that is, $0.5 c- r c=0.5 c \sin \left(0.5 \pi-\theta_{f}\right)$ or

$$
\begin{equation*}
r=0.5\left(1-\cos \theta_{f}\right) \tag{6.106}
\end{equation*}
$$

Eq. (6.105) can then be expressed as

$$
\begin{align*}
L & =\rho U^{2} \alpha_{f} c \int_{0.5 \pi-\theta_{f}}^{0.5 \pi}(1+\sin \theta) d \theta \\
& =\rho U^{2} \alpha_{f} c\left(\theta_{f}+\sin \theta_{f}\right) \tag{6.107}
\end{align*}
$$

It follows from eq. (6.106) that $r \approx 0.25 \theta_{f}^{2}$ for small $r$. Eq. (6.107) gives then

$$
\begin{equation*}
L \approx 4 \rho U^{2} c r^{1 / 2} \alpha_{f} \tag{6.108}
\end{equation*}
$$

We can introduce an efficiency coefficient $\eta_{f}$ that expresses the foil capability to provide lift relative to a flat plate with an angle of attack $\alpha_{f}$. Using eqs. (6.93) and (6.107) gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
\eta_{f}=\frac{\rho U^{2} \alpha_{f} c\left(\theta_{f}+\sin \theta_{f}\right)}{\rho U^{2} \alpha_{f} c \pi}=\frac{\theta_{f}+\sin \theta_{f}}{\pi} . \tag{6.109}
\end{equation*}
$$

Applying the asymptotic formula for small $r$, that is, eq. (6.108), we obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
\eta_{f}=\frac{4}{\pi} r^{1 / 2} \quad \text { for small } r \tag{6.110}
\end{equation*}
$$

Eqs. (6.109) and (6.110) are plotted in Figure 6.40 showing that eq. (6.110) is a reasonable approximation for $r<\approx 0.2$. Further, using, for instance, $r=0.15$ gives, respectively, $\eta_{f}=0.48$ and 0.49 for the exact and asymptotic formula. This illustrates that a flap is an efficient means of generating lift. It is not possible to use Weissinger's "quarter-three-quarter-chord" approximation to describe the effect of a flap. This would lead, for instance, to zero lift force when the flap length is less than one quarter of the chord length.

Using eq. (6.91) to calculate the hydrodynamic moment about $x=0$ gives

$$
M=-2 \rho U^{2} \alpha_{f} \int_{0.5 c-r c}^{0.5 c}\left((0.5 c)^{2}-\xi^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} d \xi
$$

Once more introducing $\theta$ as an integration variable, we get

$$
\begin{align*}
M & =-0.5 \rho U^{2} \alpha_{f} c^{2} \int_{0.5 \pi-\theta_{f}}^{0.5 \pi} \cos ^{2} \theta d \theta  \tag{6.111}\\
& =-0.25 \rho U^{2} \alpha_{f} c^{2}\left(\theta_{f}-0.5 \sin 2 \theta_{f}\right)
\end{align*}
$$

Assuming $\theta_{f}$ is small and relating $\theta_{f}$ to $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\theta_{f} & -0.5 \sin 2 \theta_{f} \approx \theta_{f}-0.5\left(2 \theta_{f}-\frac{\left(2 \theta_{f}\right)^{3}}{6}\right) \\
& =\frac{4^{2}}{3} r^{3 / 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-216.jpg?height=536&width=681&top_left_y=1674&top_left_x=839)
Figure 6.40. Flap efficiency $\eta_{f}$ as a function of the ratio $r$ between flap length and chord length.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-217.jpg?height=484&width=673&top_left_y=185&top_left_x=136)
Figure 6.41. Projections of the foil surface $S_{B}$ and vortex sheet $S_{V}$ on the $x y$-plane. These are used in the solution of the 3D linearized problem.

that is,

$$
\begin{equation*}
M=-\frac{4}{3} \rho U^{2} c^{2} r^{3 / 2} \alpha_{f} . \tag{6.112}
\end{equation*}
$$

The center of pressure $x_{C P}$ is then

$$
\begin{equation*}
x_{C P}=\frac{M}{L}=-\frac{r c}{3} . \tag{6.113}
\end{equation*}
$$

Because $r c$ is assumed small, $x_{C P}$ is close to $x=0$. It implies that we cannot simply handle the flap as an independent appended foil to the rest of the foil. The center of pressure would then be $0.75 r c$ from the trailing edge of an uncambered flap.

### 6.7 3D linear steady flow past a foil in infinite fluid

Eq. (6.41) is a representation of the velocity potential $\varphi$ for 3D nonlinear flow past a foil in infinite fluid. The problem will be linearized similarly to that in the 2D case. This is illustrated in Figure 6.41, in which the vortex sheet $S_{V}$ and the foil surface $S_{B}$ have been projected on the $x y$-plane.

The foil has a span $s$ and a local chord length $c(y)$. The incident flow velocity $U$ is along the positive $x$-axis. We will change the notation in eq. (6.41) so that the integration variable $(x, y, z)$ is replaced by $(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$ and the field point $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}\right)$ is exchanged with $(x, y, z)$. We call $I_{W}$ the linearized integral over $S_{V}^{+}$in eq. (6.41). This can be written as

$$
\begin{equation*}
I_{W}=\frac{z}{4 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} d \eta \int_{0.5 c}^{x_{E}} \frac{\left[\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}\right] d \xi}{\left[(x-\xi)^{2}+(y-\eta)^{2}+z^{2}\right]^{3 / 2}} \tag{6.114}
\end{equation*}
$$

Here $x_{E}$ corresponds to the $x$-coordinate of the longitudinal extent of the vortex sheet in the
downstream direction. This is assumed independent of $y$.

The linearized zero pressure jump condition over the vortex sheet follows from eq. (6.18) by neglecting the time-dependent part, setting the convection velocity $\boldsymbol{u}_{c}$ given by eq. (6.19) equal to $U \boldsymbol{i}$, and transferring eq. (6.18) to $z=0$. This means

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}\right)=0 \quad \text { on } z=0 \quad \text { on } S_{V} . \tag{6.115}
\end{equation*}
$$

[ $\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}$] in eq. (6.114) can then be replaced with its value at the trailing edge (T.E.). Further, in steady conditions, the vortex sheet extends to $x_{E}=\infty$. This gives

$$
\begin{align*}
I_{W}= & \frac{z}{4 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} d \eta\left[\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}\right]_{T . E .} \\
& \times \int_{0.5 c}^{\infty} \frac{d \xi}{\left[(x-\xi)^{2}+(y-\eta)^{2}+z^{2}\right]^{3 / 2}} \\
= & \frac{z}{4 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} d \eta \frac{\left[\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}\right]_{T . E .}}{\left[(y-\eta)^{2}+z^{2}\right]} \\
& \times\left\{1+\frac{x-0.5 c(\eta)}{\left[(x-0.5 c(\eta))^{2}+(y-\eta)^{2}+z^{2}\right]^{1 / 2}}\right\} \tag{6.116}
\end{align*}
$$

### 6.7.1 Prandtl's lifting line theory

We now consider Prandtl's lifting line theory. This has been presented, for instance, by Newman (1977) but a different approach will be followed here. Prandtl's lifting line theory assumes a high-aspect-ratio foil, that is, the span length is much larger than the maximum chord length. Lifting line theory is also used in the analysis of propellers (Breslin and Andersen 1994). However, because the shed vorticity behind a propeller is not located in a flat plane, as in the following analysis, the procedure becomes more complicated. However, the principle behind the analysis for a propeller is the same as described below.

We introduce far-field and near-field descriptions of the flow around the foil. The details of the transverse foil dimensions are not seen in the far-field view. The foil appears as a straight line along the $y$-axis between $y=-0.5 s$ and $0.5 s$ (Figure 6.42). The consequence is that in the far-field description of $I_{W}$, we can set $c(\eta)=0$ in eq. (6.116).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-218.jpg?height=530&width=675&top_left_y=187&top_left_x=137)
Figure 6.42. Far-field view of a high-aspect-ratio foil. This means we do not see the details of the transverse dimensions of the foil. Otherwise, the explanations are as in Figure 6.41. The foil appears to be a straight line in the $y$-axis between $y=-0.5 \mathrm{~s}$ and 0.5 s .

The details of the transverse dimensions of the foil are seen in the near-field description. The flow is locally two-dimensional in the transverse crosssectional $x z$-plane (Figure 6.43). The effect of the far-field description is a vertical inflow velocity $w_{i}$ that changes the angle of attack of the incident flow. One should note the fact that the calculated $w_{i}$ is negative; therefore, the induced velocity is downward in Figure 6.43. This reduces the angle of attack. The far-field version of eq. (6.116) is used to calculate $w_{i}$. This means both $x$ and $c$ are set equal to zero in eq. (6.116). $I_{W}$ can be re-expressed by using partial integration and noting that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{d}{d \eta} \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{z}{y-\eta}\right)=\frac{z}{(y-\eta)^{2}+z^{2}} . \tag{6.117}
\end{equation*}
$$

Using condition $\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}=0$ for $y= \pm 0.5 s$, we have

$$
\begin{gather*}
I_{W}=-\frac{1}{4 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} \frac{d}{d \eta}\left[\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}\right]_{\text {T.E. } \tan ^{-1} \frac{z}{y-\eta} d \eta}^{\text {for } x=c=0}
\end{gather*}
$$

The induced vertical velocity $w_{i}$ is then obtained by differentiating eq. (6.118) with respect to $z$ and setting $z=0$. Further, $\left[\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}\right]_{\text {T.E. }}$ can be related to the circulation $\Gamma(y)$ around the foil in the 2D flow description in Figure 6.43 (see eq. (6.15) and Figure 6.25). This gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
w_{i}=\frac{1}{4 \pi} P V \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} \frac{d \Gamma}{d \eta} \frac{d \eta}{y-\eta} . \tag{6.119}
\end{equation*}
$$

There is a circulation $\Gamma_{2 D}$ around the foil when $w_{i}$ is zero. However, $w_{i}$ causes an angle of attack $\alpha_{i}=w_{i} / U$ of the incident flow, and this changes the circulation around the foil. Using eqs. (6.62) and (6.93) gives the change in circulation due to $\alpha_{i}$ as $-U c \pi \alpha_{i}$. This gives the following equation:

$$
\Gamma(y)=\Gamma_{2 D}(y)-\pi c(y) w_{i} ;
$$

that is, noting signs, we write

$$
\begin{align*}
\Gamma(y)= & \Gamma_{2 D}(y)+\frac{1}{4} c(y) P V \\
& \times \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} \frac{d \Gamma(\eta)}{d \eta} \frac{d \eta}{\eta-y},-0.5 s<y<0.5 s \tag{6.120}
\end{align*}
$$

Eq. (6.120) can be rewritten by introducing the new variables $\theta$ and $\theta^{\prime}$ defined as

$$
\begin{equation*}
y=\frac{s}{2} \cos \theta \tag{6.121}
\end{equation*}
$$

and

$$
\begin{equation*}
\eta=\frac{s}{2} \cos \theta^{\prime} . \tag{6.122}
\end{equation*}
$$

This means that $y= \pm \frac{s}{2}$ corresponds to $\theta=0$ and $\theta=\pi$, respectively. $\Gamma$ can be expressed as the following Fourier series:

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Gamma=2 U s \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n} \sin n \theta . \tag{6.123}
\end{equation*}
$$

Because $\Gamma$ is zero for $\theta=0$ and $\pi$, Fourier series terms with $\cos n \theta$ cannot be included. Introducing the Fourier series representation gives

$$
\begin{align*}
& P V \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} \frac{d \Gamma(\eta)}{d \eta} \frac{d \eta}{\eta-y}  \tag{6.124}\\
& =-4 U \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n a_{n} P V \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\cos n \theta^{\prime} d \theta^{\prime}}{\cos \theta^{\prime}-\cos \theta}
\end{align*}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-218.jpg?height=69&width=231&top_left_y=1989&top_left_x=844)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-218.jpg?height=158&width=385&top_left_y=1940&top_left_x=1127)
Figure 6.43. Near-field view of the steady flow past a high-aspect-ratio foil in infinite fluid. The far-field 3D flow described by Figure 6.42 causes a vertical inflow velocity $w_{i}$ that changes the angle of attack of the incident flow. Note that the calculated $w_{i}$ is negative.

The Glauert integrals appearing in eq. (6.44) can be evaluated by eq. (6.81). Eq. (6.121) can then be expressed as

$$
\begin{align*}
& \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n} \sin n \theta=\frac{1}{2 U s} \Gamma_{2 D}\left(\frac{1}{2} s \cos \theta\right) \\
& -\frac{\pi}{2 s} c\left(\frac{1}{2} s \cos \theta\right) \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n a_{n} \frac{\sin n \theta}{\sin \theta}, 0<\theta<\pi \tag{6.125}
\end{align*}
$$

A linear equation system with $N$ unknowns $a_{n}$ follows by satisfying eq. (6.125) for $N$ different $\theta$-values. However, an analytical solution can be found if an uncambered lifting surface with elliptical planform is considered. In this case,

$$
\begin{equation*}
c=c_{0} \sin \theta, \tag{6.126}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $c_{0}$ is the chord at midspan. Further,

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Gamma_{2 D}=-U c \pi \alpha, \tag{6.127}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\alpha$ is the geometrical angle of attack. Using eq. (6.125) then gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
a_{1}=-\frac{\pi \alpha c_{0}}{2 s}\left(1+\frac{\pi c_{0}}{2 s}\right)^{-1} . \tag{6.128}
\end{equation*}
$$

This can be re-expressed in terms of the aspect ratio $\Lambda=s^{2} / A$, where $A=0.25 \pi c_{0} s$ is the projected area of the elliptical foil on the $x y$-plane. This gives $a_{1}=-2 \alpha /(\Lambda+2)$. The lift force $L$ on the foil is then

$$
\begin{align*}
L & =-\rho U \int_{-s / 2}^{s / 2} \Gamma(y) d y \\
& =\rho U 2 U s \frac{2 \alpha}{\Lambda+2} \cdot \frac{s}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin ^{2} \theta d \theta  \tag{6.129}\\
& =\rho U^{2} s^{2} \frac{\alpha \pi}{\Lambda+2}
\end{align*}
$$

The lift coefficient $C_{L}$ is defined as $L /\left(0.5 \rho U^{2} A\right)$, where $A=s^{2} / \Lambda$, that is,

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{L}=\frac{2 \pi \alpha}{(1+2 / \Lambda)} \tag{6.130}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\Lambda=4 s / \pi c_{0}$. Eq. (6.130) is consistent with the 2 D result $2 \pi \alpha$ when $\Lambda \rightarrow \infty$. However, when $\Lambda \rightarrow 0$, the result $\pi \Lambda \alpha$ is inconsistent with low-aspect-ratio theory, the value predicted by eq. (6.130) being twice the correct value. However, generally speaking, eq. (6.130) gives a good indication of 3D effects. Lifting line theory gives conservative estimates, and by using it, the relative

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-219.jpg?height=536&width=681&top_left_y=183&top_left_x=839)
Figure 6.44. Control volume used in expressing the drag on a foil by conservation of fluid momentum.

error is $5 \%$ at $\Lambda=8,10 \%$ at $\Lambda=4$, and $20 \%$ at $\Lambda=2$.

In 1942, the German aerodynamicist H. B. Helmbold modified eq. (6.130) to give improved predictions for low-aspect-ratio straight wings (Anderson 2001). The expression is

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{L}=\Lambda \frac{2 \pi \alpha}{2+\sqrt{\Lambda^{2}+4}} \tag{6.131}
\end{equation*}
$$

When $\Lambda \rightarrow 0$, we get $C_{L}=0.5 \pi \Lambda \alpha$. This is consistent with low-aspect-ratio theory (see section 10.3.1). Søding (1982) presented the formula

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{L}=\frac{\Lambda(\Lambda+1)}{(\Lambda+2)^{2}} 2 \pi \alpha \tag{6.132}
\end{equation*}
$$

which agrees better with the 3D results than Helmbold's formula does.

Kuchemann (1978) presents the following modification to Helmbold's equation for swept wings:

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{L}=\Lambda \frac{2 \pi \alpha \cos \gamma}{\sqrt{\Lambda^{2}+4 \cos ^{2} \gamma}+2 \cos \gamma} \tag{6.133}
\end{equation*}
$$

Here $\gamma$ means the sweep angle of the wing at the half-chord line (see Figure 6.3, in which the sweep angle is defined at the quarter-chord line).

### 6.7.2 Drag force

Drag force on the foil is derived by using conservation of fluid momentum. A fluid volume $\Omega$ exterior to the foil surface and the trailing vortex sheet is considered. $\Omega$ is bounded far away from the foil by the surfaces of a box with sides that are parallel to either the $x y-, x z-$, or $y z$-plane (Figure 6.44).

Eq. (6.116) will be used to evaluate the fluid velocity due to the vortex sheet. At the control
surface $S_{c}$ that is perpendicular to the vortex sheet far downstream of the foil, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{W}= & \frac{z}{2 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} d \eta \frac{\left[\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}\right]_{T . E .}}{\left[(y-\eta)^{2}+z^{2}\right]} \\
& \text { for } x-c / 2 \rightarrow+\infty
\end{aligned}
$$

This can be rewritten in a way similar to that used for eq. (6.119), that is,

$$
\begin{align*}
I_{W}= & \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} \frac{d \Gamma}{d \eta} \tan ^{-1} \frac{z}{y-\eta} d \eta \\
& \text { for } x-c / 2 \rightarrow+\infty \tag{6.134}
\end{align*}
$$

Here we have used $\Gamma=\left(\varphi^{-}-\varphi^{+}\right)_{\text {T.E. }}$. This shows that the flow due to the vortex sheet is twodimensional in the $y z$-plane at $S_{c}$, which means that the longitudinal velocity is $U$ at $S_{c}$. The momentum flux through the surface enclosing the control volume is therefore zero. The longitudinal pressure force acting on $S_{c}$ is

$$
\frac{\rho}{2} \iint_{S_{c}}\left[\left(\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial y}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z}\right)^{2}\right] d y d z
$$

where $\varphi$ is the same as that used in the expression of $I_{W}$. The only additional longitudinal force acting on the control volume is the force opposite the drag force $D$ on the foil. This means

$$
\begin{equation*}
D=\frac{\rho}{2} \iint_{S_{c}}\left[\left(\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial y}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z}\right)^{2}\right] d y d z \tag{6.135}
\end{equation*}
$$

This can be rewritten using the divergence theorem and by noting that $\nabla \varphi \cdot \nabla \varphi=\nabla \cdot(\varphi \nabla \varphi)$. By using the fact that $\partial \varphi / \partial z= \pm \partial \varphi / \partial n$ is continuous across the vortex sheet, the result is

$$
\begin{equation*}
D=\frac{\rho}{2} \oint \varphi \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial n} d l=-\frac{1}{2} \rho \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s}\left(\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}\right) \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z} d y \tag{6.136}
\end{equation*}
$$

The vertical velocity $\partial \varphi / \partial z$ in eq. (6.136) follows by differentiating $I_{W}$ given by eq. (6.134) with respect to $z$ and then setting $z=0$. This gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
D=\frac{\rho}{4 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} d y \Gamma(y) P V \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} \frac{d \Gamma}{d \eta} \frac{d \eta}{y-\eta} \tag{6.137}
\end{equation*}
$$

An uncambered lifting surface with elliptical planform is now considered. This means $\Gamma= 2 U s a_{1} \sin \theta$, where $a_{1}$ is given by eq. (6.128). Further, $\theta$ is defined by eq. (6.121). Using eqs. (6.81)
and (6.124) gives then

$$
\begin{aligned}
D & =\frac{\rho}{4 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} d y \Gamma(y) \pi 4 U a_{1} \\
& =\rho U a_{1} \int_{0}^{\pi} 2 U s a_{1} \sin \theta \frac{s}{2} \sin \theta d \theta \\
& =\rho U^{2} a_{1}^{2} s^{2} \frac{\pi}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding drag coefficient is

$$
C_{D}=\frac{D}{0.5 \rho U^{2} A}=\pi \Lambda a_{1}^{2}
$$

$a_{1}$ can be expressed as $-2 \alpha /(\Lambda+2)$, so

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{D}=\frac{4 \pi \alpha^{2} \Lambda}{(\Lambda+2)^{2}}=\frac{C_{L}^{2}}{\pi \Lambda} \tag{6.138}
\end{equation*}
$$

for an uncambered lifting surface with elliptical planform. Letting $\Lambda \rightarrow \infty$, this gives $C_{D}=0$, which is consistent with 2D results for a foil in infinite fluid.

The same result for the drag force can be obtained by using the Kutta-Joukowski formula for 2D flow. We consider, then, 2D flow as in Figure 6.43 and calculate $\alpha_{i}=w_{i} / U$, where $w_{i}$ is given by eq. (6.119). Here $\Gamma=2 U s a_{1} \sin \theta^{\prime}$, where $a_{1}=-2 \alpha /(\Lambda+2)$ and $\theta^{\prime}$ is defined by eq. (6.122). This leads to $\alpha_{i}=-2 \alpha /(\Lambda+2)$, which is constant along the span of the foil. There is then an incident velocity with an angle $\alpha_{i}$ relative to the $x$ axis. The magnitude of the incident velocity can be approximated as $U$. According to the KuttaJoukowski formula, the force acts perpendicularly to the inflow direction. The force magnitude can be approximated with the lift force $L$. The force acting along the $x$-axis is $-L \alpha_{i}$. Because $\alpha_{i}$ is negative, this is a drag force $D$. If $\alpha_{i}$ had been positive, it would have led to a thrust force. Using eq. (6.129) for the lift force gives

$$
D=\rho U^{2} s^{2} \frac{\alpha \pi}{\Lambda+2} \frac{2 \alpha}{\Lambda+2}
$$

and

$$
C_{D}=\frac{4 \pi \alpha^{2} \Lambda}{(\Lambda+2)^{2}}
$$

This is the same result as eq. (6.138).
These results can be generalized to include the foil camber and a flap. The 2D results with parabolic camber showed that $C_{L}=2 \pi \left[\alpha-\alpha_{0}+\eta_{f} \alpha_{f}\right]$. Here $\alpha_{0}=-2 f / c$ is the camber effect when the mean line of the foil is expressed

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-221.jpg?height=513&width=673&top_left_y=187&top_left_x=136)
Figure 6.45. Free-surface effects on steady lift for an uncambered 2D thin foil at an angle of attack. $C_{L}=$ lift coefficient, $h=$ foil submergence, $c=$ chord length, $F n_{h}=$ Froude number with $h$ as length parameter (Hough and Moran 1969).

as in eq. (6.99). Further, $\alpha_{f}$ is the flap angle (see Figure 6.39) and $\eta_{f}$ is the flap efficiency (see eq. (6.109)). The two-dimensional circulation $\Gamma_{2 D}$ in eq. (6.120) is then $-U c \pi\left(\alpha-\alpha_{0}+\eta_{f} \alpha_{f}\right)$. If $\alpha-\alpha_{0}+\eta_{f} \alpha_{f}$ does not vary along the foil span, eqs. (6.130) and (6.138) for $C_{L}$ and $C_{D}$ can be generalized by replacing $\alpha$ with $\alpha-\alpha_{0}+\eta_{f} \alpha_{f}$.

### 6.8 Steady free-surface effects on a foil

### 6.8.1 2D flow

We assume 2D steady flow and consider a thin flat foil at a submergence $h$ below the mean free surface. Infinite water depth is assumed. The linearized lift force can be expressed as in eq. (6.86). However, the circulation $\Gamma$ is influenced by the presence of the free surface. Figure 6.45 shows numerically predicted lift coefficient $C_{L}$ as a function of submergence Froude number

$$
\begin{equation*}
F n_{h}=\frac{U}{\sqrt{g h}} \tag{6.139}
\end{equation*}
$$

for different values of $h / c$. These calculations are based on a linear body boundary condition and the linear free-surface condition

$$
U^{2} \frac{\partial^{2} \varphi}{\partial x^{2}}+g \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z}=0 \quad \text { on } z=0
$$

where $\varphi$ is the velocity potential due to the foil. This is a free-surface condition similar to the one used for the Green function $G$ in eq. (4.27). The presence of the free surface causes generally lower
$C_{L}$ than for infinite fluid. An exception is small Froude numbers. The interesting Froude numbers will, in practice, be high. Consider, for instance, $U=15 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}, c=1 \mathrm{~m}$ and $h=2 \mathrm{~m}$. This gives $F n_{h}=3.4$ and about a $12 \%$ reduction in lift due to free-surface effects. However, Figure 6.45 shows that the influence of the free surface can be even higher for smaller submergences. The results are partly influenced by foil-generated free-surface waves. According to linear theory, these waves have a wavelength (see Chapter 4)

$$
\begin{equation*}
\lambda=\frac{2 \pi}{g} U^{2} . \tag{6.140}
\end{equation*}
$$

We know from linear wave theory that there is a negligible flow at a depth $\lambda$ from the free surface. We can therefore say that an object at a larger depth than $\lambda$ from the free surface causes negligible free-surface waves. This means that freesurface waves are generated when

$$
\begin{equation*}
F n_{h}>\approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \approx 0.4 . \tag{6.141}
\end{equation*}
$$

Consequently, Figure 6.45 shows large variations in $C_{L}$ with increasing values of $F n_{h}$ up to approximately $10 / \sqrt{h / c}$ or $U / \sqrt{g c} \approx 10$. When $F n_{h}> 10 / \sqrt{h / c}, C_{L}$ is nearly independent of $F n_{h}$. The same results can then be predicted by neglecting gravity and using the dynamic free-surface condition $\varphi=0$, where $\varphi$ is the velocity potential due to the foil. This is often referred to as the biplane approximation and implies that the fluid velocity due to the foil is vertical at the free surface. The case is discussed more, later in the text.

When the Froude number is very small, the free surface acts like a rigid wall. The problem is then similar to a lifting wing close to the ground. The wing-in-ground (WIG) effect causes the lift to increase with decreasing distance of the foil from the ground. The results in Figure 6.45 show this. A WIG vehicle, as presented in Figure 1.11, takes advantage of this effect.

The behavior when $F n_{h} \rightarrow 0$ or $F n_{h}>10 / \sqrt{h / c}$ follows by a simple analysis based on Weissinger's quarter-three-quarter-chord approximation (see section 6.6.4). We start out with $F n_{h} \rightarrow 0$ and represent the flow due to the foil by two vortices with opposite circulations $\Gamma$. One vortex has a center in the foil at a distance $c / 4$ from the leading edge. The other vortex has a center at the image point about the mean free surface (see Figure 6.46). Note that we have used the opposite

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-222.jpg?height=388&width=673&top_left_y=185&top_left_x=138)
Figure 6.46. Approximate flow around a foil near the ground. Also representative for submerged foil near the free surface when the Froude number is asymptotically small.

circulation direction relative to the previous definition. The reason is that the sign of the circulation used in Figure 6.46 gives a direct illustration that the flow velocity increases on the suction side of the foil. Because the two vortices have opposite signs, the rigid free-surface condition is satisfied. According to the Weissinger approximation, the body boundary condition has to be satisfied only at one point, that is, at a distance $3 c / 4$ from the leading edge. The image vortex effectively causes an increase in the angle of attack at this point. This means a higher $C_{L}$-value. The closer the image vortex, the higher $C_{L}$. We have earlier shown that the Weissinger approximation is appropriate for steady flow around a 2D foil with angle of attack and parabolic camber in infinite fluid. However, it does not apply to a foil with a flap. Let us examine whether it can account for the free-surface effect when $F n_{h} \rightarrow 0$ for a foil with angle of attack and camber. The body boundary condition gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{\Gamma}{\pi c}-\frac{0.5 c \Gamma}{2 \pi\left(4 h^{2}+0.25 c^{2}\right)}=U(\alpha+2 f / c), \tag{6.142}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\alpha$ and $f$ are defined by eq. (6.99). Solving eq. (6.142) for $\Gamma$ and using the Kutta-Joukowski formula (see eq. (6.62)), we can evaluate the lift on the foil. The result of the analysis is that the lift coefficient can be written as

$$
\begin{align*}
C_{L}\left(\frac{h}{c}\right) & =C_{L}\left(\frac{h}{c}=\infty\right)\left[1+\frac{1}{16}\left(\frac{c}{h}\right)^{2}\right] \\
& \text { when } F n_{h} \rightarrow 0 \tag{6.143}
\end{align*}
$$

Eq. (6.143) shows the correct trend that the lift increases strongly for small $h / c$-values, but the infinite predicted lift for $h / c=0$ must obviously be wrong. The ratio between $C_{L}$ and its infinite fluid
value in the case of the lowest $F n_{h}$-value in Figure 6.45 is, respectively, 1.1 and 1.05 for $h / c=1.0$ and 2.0. The corresponding values by using eq. (6.143) are 1.06 and 1.02.

When $F n_{h}>10 / \sqrt{h / c}$, the only difference in the analysis is that the two vortices have the same sign (Figure 6.47). This ensures that the dynamic free-surface condition $\varphi=0$ is satisfied. The analysis gives

$$
\begin{align*}
C_{L}\left(\frac{h}{c}\right) & =C_{L}\left(\frac{h}{c}=\infty\right) \cdot\left[\frac{1+16(h / c)^{2}}{2+16(h / c)^{2}}\right] \\
& \text { when } F n_{h}>10 / \sqrt{h / c} \tag{6.144}
\end{align*}
$$

This illustrates that $C_{L}$ decreases with decreasing distance of the foil from the free surface. Eq. (6.144) predicts $C_{L} / C_{L}(h / c=\infty)$ equal to 0.83 and 0.94 for, respectively, $h / c=0.5$ and 1.0. This agrees reasonably with Figure 6.45. When $h / c=0$, eq. (6.144) gives $C_{L} / C_{L}(h / c=\infty)=0.5$. This is consistent with linear theory for a planing foil on the free surface. In reality, cavitation and ventilation may happen to a foil at high Froude number very close to the free surface (see discussion associated with eq. (6.2)). This may cause a significant reduction of the lift. $C_{L}$ of a supercavitating thin flat foil in infinite fluid is $0.5 \pi \alpha$, whereas the corresponding value with no cavitation and ventilation is $2 \pi \alpha$.

Kochin et al. (1964) have given expressions for the wave resistance. By using linear theory, we can divide the flow into a thickness and lifting problem, which can be solved by using, respectively, source (sink) and vortex distributions along the foil (see Figure 6.37). Both effects cause wave resistance. We consider first the lifting problem. The wave resistance can be expressed as

$$
\begin{equation*}
R_{W \Gamma}=\frac{\rho g \Gamma^{2}}{U^{2}} \exp \left(-2 / F n_{h}^{2}\right) . \tag{6.145}
\end{equation*}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-222.jpg?height=344&width=677&top_left_y=1871&top_left_x=841)
Figure 6.47. Approximate flow around a foil below the free surface when the Froude number is very high.

$\frac{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{DWT}}}{\mathrm{c}_{\mathrm{L}}^{2}} \frac{\mathrm{~h}}{\mathrm{c}}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-223.jpg?height=530&width=656&top_left_y=255&top_left_x=154)
Figure 6.48. Wave resistance due to lift effects on a 2D foil with submergence $h$ and chord length $c$, expressed in terms of drag coefficient $C_{D W \Gamma}$ as a function of submergence Froude number $F n_{h} . C_{L}$ is the lift coefficient for the foil.

This means

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{D W \Gamma}=\frac{R_{W \Gamma}}{0.5 \rho U^{2} c}=\frac{g \Gamma^{2}}{0.5 U^{4} c} \exp \left(-2 / F n_{h}^{2}\right) . \tag{6.146}
\end{equation*}
$$

We introduce now the lift coefficient $C_{L}= L /\left(0.5 \rho U^{2} c\right)$ and evaluate the lift force $L$ by eq. (6.86). This means

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{L}^{2}=\frac{\Gamma^{2}}{0.25 U^{2} c^{2}} . \tag{6.147}
\end{equation*}
$$

Combining eqs. (6.146) and (6.147) gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{C_{D W \Gamma}}{C_{L}^{2}}=\frac{0.5}{F n_{h}^{2}}\left(\frac{c}{h}\right) \exp \left(-2 / F n_{h}^{2}\right) . \tag{6.148}
\end{equation*}
$$

This expression is plotted in Figure 6.48. The maximum value of $C_{D W \Gamma} / C_{L}^{2}$ occurs at $F n_{h}=\sqrt{2}$ and is equal to $0.25 e^{-1} c / h=0.092 c / h$.

The thickness of a foil also causes a wave resistance component $R_{W S}$. This is similar to what we described in Chapter 4 for ships. Kochin et al. (1964) have presented a formula for a 2D foil with elliptical cross section and without lift. The formula is

$$
\begin{align*}
R_{W S}= & \pi^{2} \rho g t^{2} \frac{c+t}{c-t} e^{-2 / F n_{h}^{2}} J_{1}^{2} \\
& \times\left[\frac{c}{2 h} \frac{1}{F n_{h}^{2}}\left(1-\left(\frac{t}{c}\right)^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}\right] \tag{6.149}
\end{align*}
$$

Here, $t$ is the thickness of the foil and $J_{1}$ is the Bessel function of the first kind and order one
(Abramowitz and Stegun 1964). Eq. (6.149) is presented in Figure 6.49 as a function of submergence Froude number $F n_{h}$ for difference ratios between the submergence $h$ and the chord length $c$. The calculations are done for $t / c=0.075$, but $R_{W S} / \rho g t^{2}$ is not very sensitive to $t / c$.

In order to quantify the importance of $R_{W S}$, we have compared it with the viscous resistance $R_{V}$ obtained by using eq. (2.90). The chord length and the submergence were both chosen as 1 m , that is, $h / c=1$. In the calculations, the foil thickness is 0.075 m and the kinematic viscosity coefficient is $1.35 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. The ratio $\left(R_{W S}+R_{V}\right) / R_{V}$ is 1.026 for $U=5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ and decreases rapidly with increasing $U$. This indicates that wave resistance due to thickness effect is small. The same is not true for wave resistance due to lift effects. It is not rigorous to separate the wave resistance due thickness and lifting effects even if we can separate the flow due to thickness and lifting effects. The reason is that the wave resistance can be related to the square of the downstream wave amplitude generated by the foil. This gives interaction terms. However, in the following text, we will assume that the wave resistance due to lifting effects dominates and neglect the thickness effect.

A consequence of wave resistance $R_{W}$ is that the foil generates steady regular waves with amplitude $A$ far downstream of the foil. By using energy conservation (Newman 1977), it can be shown that

$$
\begin{equation*}
R_{W}=\frac{\rho g}{4} A^{2} . \tag{6.150}
\end{equation*}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-223.jpg?height=585&width=673&top_left_y=1551&top_left_x=841)
Figure 6.49. Wave resistance $R_{W S}$ due to the thickness effect of a 2D foil with elliptical cross section at submergence $h . c=$ chord length, $t=$ foil thickness, $t / c=$ 0.075 .

### 6.8.2 3D flow

The free surface will affect the 3D steady flow around a foil. The free-surface effect on the lift has been presented earlier for 2D steady flow (see Figure 6.45).

Eqs. (6.143) and (6.144) can be combined with the lifting line theory to account for the free surface when $F n_{h} \rightarrow 0$ and $F n_{h} \rightarrow \infty$. If high Froude number is considered, $\Gamma_{2 D}$ given by eq. (6.127) can be generalized to $-U c \pi \alpha\left(1+16(h / c)^{2}\right) / \left(2+16(h / c)^{2}\right)$. This implies that $C_{L}$ of an elliptical planform also satisfies eq. (6.144). This gives that $C_{L} / C_{L}(h / c=4)$ is $0.67,0.84$, and 0.95 for, respectively, $h / c=0.25,0.5$, and1.0. This is in reasonable agreement with the experimental and theoretical results by van Walree (1999) for large $F n_{h}$. He studied a rectangular foil with aspect ratio 6 ; however, his small $F n_{h}$ results do not agree so well with the asymptotic results for an elliptical planform when $F n_{h} \rightarrow 0$.

The formula for the drag coefficient $C_{D}$ of a horizontal foil with elliptic loading based on potential flow has been presented by Breslin (1957). Linearized free-surface conditions are assumed. When the Froude number is asymptotically large, we can write

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{C_{D}}{C_{L}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\pi \Lambda}+\frac{\sigma(\lambda)}{\pi \Lambda}, \quad F n_{h} \rightarrow \infty \tag{6.151}
\end{equation*}
$$

where

$$
\begin{align*}
\sigma(\lambda)= & 1-\frac{4}{\pi} \lambda \sqrt{1+\lambda^{2}}\left[K\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\lambda^{2}}}\right)\right. \\
& \left.-E\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\lambda^{2}}}\right)\right] \tag{6.152}
\end{align*}
$$

and $\lambda=2 h / s$, with $s$ as the foil span. Here $K$ and $E$ are complete elliptic integrals of the first and second kind. The aspect ratio $\Lambda$ for an elliptical foil can be expressed as

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Lambda=\frac{4}{\pi} \frac{s}{c_{o}}, \tag{6.153}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $c_{o}$ is maximum chord length. We can derive eq. (6.151) for the drag force by conservation of fluid momentum and by following a procedure similar to the one in section 6.7.2 for a foil in infinite fluid. The upper surface of the control volume will coincide with the mean free surface. The drag force $D$ can be expressed as in eq. (6.135). The difference now is that the vertical control surfaces

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-224.jpg?height=793&width=679&top_left_y=200&top_left_x=841)
Figure 6.50. High Froude number flow around a 3D foil. (a) The solution is represented in terms of an image flow above the free surface. (b) Representation of the vortex sheet and the image vortex sheet in the $y z$-plane far downstream the foil.

extend only up to the mean free surface. By using the divergence theorem as in eq. (6.136), it follows that

$$
\begin{equation*}
D=-\frac{1}{2} \rho \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s}\left(\varphi^{+}-\varphi^{-}\right) \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z} d y \tag{6.154}
\end{equation*}
$$

where $\partial \varphi / \partial z$ is the vertical fluid velocity at the intersection between $S_{C}$ and the vortex sheet behind the foil. The difference is now in the way $\partial \varphi / \partial z$ is evaluated. We can express a solution for $\partial \varphi / \partial z$ by imagining that the flow around the foil at high Froude number is the same as the flow around the foil and an image foil above the free surface. The image foil causes a vortex sheet with the same vorticity as in the vortex sheet behind the foil (see Figure 6.50). This image system ensures that the high Froude number free-surface condition $\varphi=0$ on the mean free surface is satisfied. Here $\varphi$ is the velocity potential caused by the foil. This is similar to the 2D case shown in Figure 6.47.
$\partial \varphi / \partial z$ in eq. (6.154) consists of two parts. The first part is the result of the vortex sheet behind the foil. The expression is the same as that used in eq. (6.137). The second contribution comes from the image vortex sheet above the mean free
surface. This can be expressed as the vertical velocity induced by a two-dimensional distribution of vortices along the image vortex sheet, that is, similar to the evaluation of $\partial \varphi / \partial z$ from eq. (6.134). We get

$$
\begin{equation*}
w_{i_{2}}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} \frac{d \Gamma}{d \eta} \frac{y-\eta}{(y-\eta)^{2}+4 h^{2}} d \eta . \tag{6.155}
\end{equation*}
$$

We introduce now an elliptical circulation distribution along the span of the foil, that is,

$$
\begin{equation*}
\Gamma=\Gamma_{0}\left(1-\left(\frac{2 \eta}{s}\right)^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} . \tag{6.156}
\end{equation*}
$$

If a high-aspect-ratio plane foil is considered, Prandtl's lifting theory (see section 6.7.1) shows that an elliptical planform implies an elliptical circulation distribution. However, eq. (6.156) is also possible to achieve with other planforms. By integrating eq. (6.155) by parts we find that

$$
\begin{align*}
w_{i_{2}}= & -\frac{\Gamma_{0}}{2 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s}\left(1-\left(\frac{2 \eta}{s}\right)^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} \\
& \times \frac{(y-\eta)^{2}-4 h^{2}}{\left[(y-\eta)^{2}+4 h^{2}\right]^{2}} d \eta . \tag{6.157}
\end{align*}
$$

Introducing $y=y_{1} \frac{s}{2}$ and $\eta=y_{2} \frac{s}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
w_{i_{2}}=-\frac{\Gamma_{0}}{\pi s} \int_{-1}^{1}\left(1-y_{2}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} \frac{\left[\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{16 h^{2}}{s^{2}}\right]}{\left[\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right)^{2}+\frac{16 h^{2}}{s^{2}}\right]^{2}} d y_{2} . \tag{6.158}
\end{equation*}
$$

By inserting $\partial \varphi / \partial z$ into eq. (6.154), we have

$$
\begin{align*}
D= & \frac{\rho}{4 \pi} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} d y \Gamma(\mathrm{y}) P V \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} \frac{d \Gamma}{d \eta} \frac{d \eta}{y-\eta} \\
& +D_{2} \tag{6.159}
\end{align*}
$$

The first term leads to the expression for the drag in infinite fluid (see eq. (6.138)) and is the first term on the right-hand side of eq. (6.151). The second term, $D_{2}$, is the result of the image vortex sheet and can be expressed as

$$
\begin{align*}
D_{2} & =\frac{\rho}{2} \int_{-0.5 s}^{0.5 s} \Gamma(y) w_{i_{2}}(y) d y \\
& =\frac{\rho s}{4} \Gamma_{0} \int_{-1}^{1}\left(1-y_{1}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} w_{i_{2}}\left(y_{1}\right) d y_{1}  \tag{6.160}\\
& =\rho \Gamma_{0}^{2} \frac{\pi}{8} \sigma
\end{align*}
$$

where

$$
\begin{align*}
\sigma= & -\frac{2}{\pi^{2}} \int_{-1}^{1} d y_{1}\left(1-y_{1}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} \\
& \times \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{\left[\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{16 h^{2}}{s^{2}}\right]\left(1-y_{2}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}}{\left[\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right)^{2}+\frac{16 h^{2}}{s^{2}}\right]^{2}} d y_{2} . \tag{6.161}
\end{align*}
$$

$D_{2}$ can be expressed in terms of the lift, which is

$$
\begin{equation*}
L=-\rho U \Gamma_{0} \int_{-s / 2}^{s / 2}\left(1-\left(\frac{2 y}{s}\right)^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} d y=-\rho U \Gamma_{0} \frac{\pi s}{4} \tag{6.162}
\end{equation*}
$$

for elliptical loading. The lift coefficient is

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{L}=\frac{L}{0.5 \rho U^{2} A}=-\frac{\pi}{2} \frac{\Gamma_{0} s}{U A} . \tag{6.163}
\end{equation*}
$$

The drag coefficient associated with $D_{2}$ is

$$
\begin{equation*}
C_{D_{2}}=\frac{D_{2}}{0.5 \rho U^{2} A}=\frac{\rho \Gamma_{0}^{2} \frac{\pi}{8} \sigma}{0.5 \rho U^{2} A} . \tag{6.164}
\end{equation*}
$$

Using eq. (6.163) to express $\Gamma_{0} / U$ gives

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{C_{D_{2}}}{C_{L}^{2}}=\frac{\sigma}{\pi \Lambda} . \tag{6.165}
\end{equation*}
$$

This means the same as the second term in eq. (6.151) if $\sigma$ given by eq. (6.161) is the same as eq. (6.152). To show this equivalence analytically is not trivial. However, numerical calculations give the same answer from the two expressions.

When the Froude number goes to zero, we can follow a similar analysis as for infinite Froude number. However, the circulation around the image foil and the vorticity in the image vortex sheet must now be opposite the circulation around the foil and to the vorticity in the vortex sheet, respectively, in order to satisfy the rigid free-surface condition. The analogue case for 2D flow was illustrated in Figure 6.48. The analysis gives that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{C_{D}}{C_{L}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\pi \Lambda}-\frac{\sigma(\lambda)}{\pi \Lambda}, \quad F n_{h} \rightarrow 0 \tag{6.166}
\end{equation*}
$$

when the Froude number is asymptotically small.
Eqs. (6.151) and (6.166) are presented in Figure 6.51 as a function of $h / c$ when the aspect ratio is 6. The asymptotic value for $h / c \rightarrow \infty$ is 0.053 . We note that decreasing $h / c$ increases $C_{D}$ in the infinite Froude number case. The opposite trend happens in the low Froude number case. The results for infinite Froude number are in good agreement

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-226.jpg?height=654&width=673&top_left_y=191&top_left_x=136)
Figure 6.51. Theoretical drag coefficient $C_{D}$ for a horizontal foil with elliptical loading as a function of ratio between submergence $h$ and maximum chord length $c$ at infinite and zero Froude numbers. The aspect ratio is 6 .

with the results by van Walree (1999) even if those results are for a rectangular foil.

Breslin's formula for $C_{D}$ for any Froude number is

$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{C_{D}}{C_{L}^{2}}= & \frac{1}{\pi \Lambda}-\frac{\sigma(\lambda)}{\pi \Lambda}+\frac{8}{\pi \Lambda} \\
& \times \int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \frac{J_{1}^{2}\left(0.5 v s \sec ^{2} \theta \sin \theta\right) e^{-2 v h \sec ^{2} \theta}}{\sin ^{2} \theta \cos \theta} d \theta \tag{6.167}
\end{align*}
$$

Here $J_{1}$ is a Bessel function of the first kind and $v= g / U^{2}$. Eq. (6.167) accounts for both transverse and divergent waves and is based on using the linear free-surface condition given by eq. (4.27) for the flow caused by foil.

Results for aspect ratio 6 and different $h / c$ values are presented in Figure 6.52. These results are in reasonable agreement with the experimental and numerical results for a rectangular foil with the same aspect ratio as the one presented by van Walree (1999). One exception is for the largest $C_{D} / C_{L}^{2}$-values occurring at $h / c=0.25$. Because the foil is then close to the free surface, nonlinear free-surface effects may matter. An important contribution to the peak values of $C_{D} / C_{L}^{2}$ presented in Figure 6.52 is the result of transverse waves. This is illustrated in Figure 6.53 for the elliptical foil at $h / c=1.0$ by separating the con-

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-226.jpg?height=567&width=671&top_left_y=193&top_left_x=843)
Figure 6.52. Drag coefficient $C_{D}$ of a horizontal foil with elliptical loading, submergence $h$, and maximum chord length $c$ presented as a function of submergence Froude number $F n_{h}$. Aspect ratio $=6$.

tribution from transverse waves. This is estimated by integrating from 0 to $\sin ^{-1}(1 / \sqrt{3})$ in the integral in eq. (6.167). We note that the effect of the transverse waves is small when $F n_{h}>\approx 4.0$. The effect of the divergent waves will then contribute. However, the results are quite close to the drag at infinite Froude number when $F n_{h}>\approx 4.0$. The latter does not include wave effects. The 2D results presented in Figure 6.48 contain only the effect of transverse waves and, to a large extent, can explain

Figure 6.53. Drag coefficient $C_{D}$ of a horizontal foil with elliptical loading at submergence $(h)$ to maximum chord length (c) ratio 1 presented as a function of submergence Froude number $F n_{h}$. Aspect ratio = 6. The contribution to $C_{D}$ from transverse waves is illustrated.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/425baa0a-eab6-4584-a37e-072cea045b9b-227.jpg?height=268&width=673&top_left_y=193&top_left_x=136)
Figure 6.54. Tandem arrangement of two foils with equal submergence $h$.
